title: All Permutations in Sorted Order
description:
Given a word made of distinct lowercase letters, print every permutation of its letters in lexicographic (dictionary) order. Use recursion: fix one letter, then permute the rest.

  • 1 ≤ length ≤ 6
  • All letters are different.

Input

A single line containing the word.

Output

Print all permutations, one per line, in increasing lexicographic order.

Example

Input:

abc

Output:

abc
acb
bac
bca
cab
cba

title: Subsets in Lexicographic Order
description:
Given n distinct integers, print all 2n subsets. Inside each subset the numbers are listed in increasing order. The subsets themselves are listed in lexicographic order when compared as sequences of integers (a sequence that is a proper prefix of another comes first), so the empty subset is always first.

  • 1 ≤ n ≤ 10
  • -100 ≤ values ≤ 100, all distinct

Input

The first line contains n. The second line contains n space-separated distinct integers (in any order).

Output

Print each subset on its own line, written as { + the numbers separated by single spaces + }. The empty subset is printed as {}.

Example

Input:

3
1 2 3

Output:

{}
{1}
{1 2}
{1 2 3}
{1 3}
{2}
{2 3}
{3}
solution:
n = int(input())
a = sorted(map(int, input().split()))
out = []
def go(start, cur):
    out.append("{" + " ".join(map(str, cur)) + "}")
    for i in range(start, n):
        cur.append(a[i])
        go(i + 1, cur)
        cur.pop()
go(0, [])
print("\n".join(out))

title: Combinations n Choose k
description:
Print every way to choose k different numbers from 1, 2, ..., n. Each combination is written in increasing order, and the combinations are listed in lexicographic order. After the list, print the total number of combinations.

  • 1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ 12

Input

A single line with two integers n and k.

Output

One combination per line, numbers separated by single spaces. The last line is Total: X where X is the number of combinations.

Example

Input:

4 2

Output:

1 2
1 3
1 4
2 3
2 4
3 4
Total: 6
solution:
n, k = map(int, input().split())
res = []
def go(start, cur):
    if len(cur) == k:
        res.append(" ".join(map(str, cur)))
        return
    for x in range(start, n - (k - len(cur)) + 2):
        cur.append(x)
        go(x + 1, cur)
        cur.pop()
go(1, [])
print("\n".join(res))
print("Total:", len(res))

title: N-Queens Solution Count
description:
Count the number of ways to place n queens on an n × n chessboard so that no two queens attack each other (no two share a row, a column or a diagonal).

  • 1 ≤ n ≤ 11
  • Trying all placements is far too slow for the larger boards; use backtracking that places one queen per row and prunes attacked columns/diagonals.

Input

A single integer n.

Output

Print the number of valid arrangements.

Example

Input:

4

Output:

2
solution:
n = int(input())
full = (1 << n) - 1
def go(cols, d1, d2):
    if cols == full:
        return 1
    c = 0
    avail = full & ~(cols | d1 | d2)
    while avail:
        b = avail & -avail
        avail -= b
        c += go(cols | b, ((d1 | b) << 1) & full, (d2 | b) >> 1)
    return c
print(go(0, 0, 0))

title: Sudoku Solver
description:
Solve a standard 9×9 Sudoku. Fill every empty cell with a digit 1–9 so that each row, each column and each of the nine 3×3 boxes contains every digit exactly once.

  • Every given puzzle has exactly one solution.
  • Some puzzles are very hard (17 clues or designed against naive backtracking). A plain cell-by-cell backtracking without good pruning may be too slow; choose the empty cell with the fewest candidates first and track used digits per row/column/box.
  • A puzzle may already be complete.

Input

Nine lines, each containing exactly 9 digits with no spaces. A 0 marks an empty cell.

Output

Print the solved grid as nine lines of 9 digits each.

Example

Input:

530070000
600195000
098000060
800060003
400803001
700020006
060000280
000419005
000080079

Output:

534678912
672195348
198342567
859761423
426853791
713924856
961537284
287419635
345286179
solution:
g = [list(map(int, input().strip())) for _ in range(9)]
rows = [0] * 9
cols = [0] * 9
boxes = [0] * 9
empty = []
for r in range(9):
    for c in range(9):
        v = g[r][c]
        if v:
            b = 1 << v
            rows[r] |= b
            cols[c] |= b
            boxes[r // 3 * 3 + c // 3] |= b
        else:
            empty.append((r, c))
ALL = 0b1111111110
def solve():
    best = None
    bestcnt = 10
    for r, c in empty:
        if g[r][c] == 0:
            m = ALL & ~(rows[r] | cols[c] | boxes[r // 3 * 3 + c // 3])
            k = bin(m).count("1")
            if k < bestcnt:
                bestcnt = k
                best = (r, c, m)
                if k <= 1:
                    break
    if best is None:
        return True
    r, c, m = best
    bi = r // 3 * 3 + c // 3
    while m:
        b = m & -m
        m -= b
        g[r][c] = b.bit_length() - 1
        rows[r] |= b
        cols[c] |= b
        boxes[bi] |= b
        if solve():
            return True
        rows[r] ^= b
        cols[c] ^= b
        boxes[bi] ^= b
        g[r][c] = 0
    return False
solve()
for row in g:
    print("".join(map(str, row)))

title: Tower of Hanoi Moves
description:
There are three pegs A, B and C. Disks 1 (smallest) to n (largest) start on peg A. Move the whole tower to peg C using the minimum number of moves; a larger disk may never sit on a smaller one. Use the standard recursive solution: move n-1 disks from the source to the auxiliary peg, move disk n to the target, then move the n-1 disks from the auxiliary peg to the target.

  • 1 ≤ n ≤ 10

Input

A single integer n.

Output

Print each move on its own line as Move disk D from X to Y, in order. Finally print Total moves: M.

Example

Input:

2

Output:

Move disk 1 from A to B
Move disk 2 from A to C
Move disk 1 from B to C
Total moves: 3
solution:
n = int(input())
moves = []
def hanoi(k, src, aux, dst):
    if k == 0:
        return
    hanoi(k - 1, src, dst, aux)
    moves.append("Move disk %d from %s to %s" % (k, src, dst))
    hanoi(k - 1, aux, src, dst)
hanoi(n, "A", "B", "C")
print("\n".join(moves))
print("Total moves:", len(moves))

title: Combination Sum
description:
Given a list of distinct positive integers and a target, find every combination of the numbers whose sum equals the target. Each number may be used any number of times. Two combinations are the same if they use the same numbers the same number of times.

  • 1 ≤ n ≤ 10
  • 2 ≤ each number ≤ 40
  • 1 ≤ target ≤ 45

Input

The first line contains n and target. The second line contains the n numbers.

Output

Print each combination on its own line with its numbers in non-decreasing order separated by single spaces. List combinations in lexicographic order (compare as integer sequences). If no combination exists print NONE.

Example

Input:

4 7
2 3 6 7

Output:

2 2 3
7
solution:
n, t = map(int, input().split())
a = sorted(map(int, input().split()))
res = []
def go(start, rem, cur):
    if rem == 0:
        res.append(" ".join(map(str, cur)))
        return
    for i in range(start, n):
        if a[i] > rem:
            break
        cur.append(a[i])
        go(i, rem - a[i], cur)
        cur.pop()
go(0, t, [])
print("\n".join(res) if res else "NONE")

title: Reflected Gray Code
description:
The reflected binary Gray code of n bits is built recursively: for n = 1 it is 0, 1. For larger n, take the list for n-1 bits and prefix every code with 0, then take the same list in reverse and prefix every code with 1. Consecutive codes differ in exactly one bit.

  • 1 ≤ n ≤ 10

Input

A single integer n.

Output

Print the 2n codes in order, one per line, each as an n-character binary string.

Example

Input:

2

Output:

00
01
11
10
solution:
n = int(input())
def gray(k):
    if k == 1:
        return ["0", "1"]
    prev = gray(k - 1)
    return ["0" + c for c in prev] + ["1" + c for c in reversed(prev)]
print("\n".join(gray(n)))

title: Permutations with Duplicates
description:
Given a list of integers that may contain duplicates, print every distinct permutation exactly once, in lexicographic order (compare as integer sequences), followed by the number of distinct permutations.

  • 1 ≤ n ≤ 8
  • -50 ≤ values ≤ 50
  • Generating all n! orderings and removing duplicates afterwards works for small inputs but wastes time; skip equal choices during the recursion instead.

Input

The first line contains n. The second line contains n space-separated integers.

Output

Print each distinct permutation on its own line with numbers separated by single spaces, then a final line Total: X.

Example

Input:

3
1 1 2

Output:

1 1 2
1 2 1
2 1 1
Total: 3
solution:
n = int(input())
a = sorted(map(int, input().split()))
used = [False] * n
res = []
cur = []
def go():
    if len(cur) == n:
        res.append(" ".join(map(str, cur)))
        return
    for i in range(n):
        if used[i] or (i > 0 and a[i] == a[i - 1] and not used[i - 1]):
            continue
        used[i] = True
        cur.append(a[i])
        go()
        cur.pop()
        used[i] = False
go()
print("\n".join(res))
print("Total:", len(res))

title: Rat in a Maze: All Paths
description:
A rat starts at the top-left cell (0, 0) of an N × N maze and wants to reach the bottom-right cell (N-1, N-1). A cell with 1 is open and 0 is blocked. In one step the rat moves Up, Down, Left or Right to an open cell, and it may not visit a cell twice in the same path.

Count all such paths and find the alphabetically smallest one, written as the string of moves (letters compared alphabetically, so D < L < R < U).

  • 2 ≤ N ≤ 5

Input

The first line contains N. The next N lines each contain N space-separated values (0 or 1).

Output

Print the number of paths on the first line. If it is greater than 0, print the alphabetically smallest path on the second line. If the start or end cell is blocked, the answer is 0.

Example

Input:

4
1 0 0 0
1 1 0 1
1 1 0 0
0 1 1 1

Output:

2
DDRDRR
solution:
n = int(input())
g = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(n)]
seen = [[False] * n for _ in range(n)]
count = 0
best = None
moves = (("D", 1, 0), ("L", 0, -1), ("R", 0, 1), ("U", -1, 0))
path = []
def go(r, c):
    global count, best
    if r == n - 1 and c == n - 1:
        count += 1
        if best is None:
            best = "".join(path)
        return
    seen[r][c] = True
    for ch, dr, dc in moves:
        nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
        if 0 <= nr < n and 0 <= nc < n and g[nr][nc] == 1 and not seen[nr][nc]:
            path.append(ch)
            go(nr, nc)
            path.pop()
    seen[r][c] = False
if g[0][0] == 1 and g[n - 1][n - 1] == 1:
    go(0, 0)
print(count)
if count:
    print(best)

title: K-th Permutation Sequence
description:
List all permutations of 1, 2, ..., n in lexicographic order and number them starting from 1. Print the k-th one.

  • 1 ≤ n ≤ 20
  • 1 ≤ k ≤ n!
  • For large n there are far too many permutations to generate; determine each position directly using factorials.

Input

A single line with two integers n and k.

Output

Print the k-th permutation, numbers separated by single spaces.

Example

Input:

3 3

Output:

2 1 3
solution:
n, k = map(int, input().split())
nums = list(range(1, n + 1))
fact = [1] * (n + 1)
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    fact[i] = fact[i - 1] * i
k -= 1
res = []
for i in range(n, 0, -1):
    idx = k // fact[i - 1]
    k %= fact[i - 1]
    res.append(nums.pop(idx))
print(" ".join(map(str, res)))

title: Expression Add Operators
description:
Given a string of digits and a target value, insert the binary operators +, - or * between some of the digits (or nothing, which joins digits into a longer number) so that the resulting expression evaluates to the target. Normal precedence applies: * is done before + and -.

  • 1 ≤ number of digits ≤ 9
  • -109 ≤ target ≤ 109
  • An operand may not have leading zeros: 05 is not allowed, but a single 0 is.
  • No unary minus; the digit order may not change.
  • Evaluate expressions incrementally during the search (keep the value of the last multiplied term) instead of building and evaluating each string separately.

Input

The first line contains the digit string. The second line contains the target.

Output

Print the number of valid expressions on the first line, then every valid expression on its own line (no spaces), sorted in ASCII order (in ASCII * < + < - < digits).

Example

Input:

123
6

Output:

2
1*2*3
1+2+3

title: Grid Paths with Diagonal Steps
description:
A token starts at the top-left cell of an R × C grid and must reach the bottom-right cell. From cell (r, c) it may step right to (r, c+1), down to (r+1, c) or diagonally to (r+1, c+1). Cells marked # are walls and cannot be entered. Count the number of different paths modulo 1000000007.

Think recursively: the number of paths from a cell is the sum of the paths from its three successors — but memoize, or the recursion explodes.

  • 1 ≤ R, C ≤ 100
  • If the start or the end cell is a wall the answer is 0. A 1×1 open grid has exactly 1 path.

Input

The first line contains R and C. The next R lines each contain C characters, . or #.

Output

Print the number of paths modulo 1000000007.

Example

Input:

3 3
...
.#.
...

Output:

4

description:
Given a string of letters and digits, every letter may be written either in lowercase or uppercase. Print all different strings that can be produced this way. Digits stay unchanged.

  • 1 ≤ length ≤ 12, at most 10 letters

Input

A single line containing the string.

Output

Print every resulting string once, one per line, sorted in ASCII order (uppercase letters come before lowercase letters).

Example

Input:

s = input().strip()

title: Partition into K Equal-Sum Groups
description:
Decide whether a list of positive integers can be split into exactly k non-empty groups such that every number belongs to exactly one group and all groups have the same sum.

  • 1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ 14
  • 1 ≤ values ≤ 10000
  • Trying every assignment of numbers to groups (kn) is too slow. Use backtracking with strong pruning or a bitmask over used numbers.

Input

The first line contains n and k. The second line contains the n integers.

Output

Print YES if such a split exists, otherwise NO.

Example

Input:

7 4
4 3 2 3 5 2 1

Output:

YES

title: Fair Cookie Distribution
description:
There are n bags of cookies; bag i holds ai cookies. Give every bag (unopened) to one of k children. The unfairness of a distribution is the largest total number of cookies received by a single child. Print the minimum possible unfairness. A child may receive no bags.

  • 1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ 10
  • 1 ≤ ai ≤ 100000
  • Plain enumeration of all kn distributions is too slow for the biggest cases. Prune: sort the bags in decreasing order, stop a branch as soon as a child reaches the best answer found so far, and do not try two children that currently hold the same amount.

Input

The first line contains n and k. The second line contains the n bag sizes.

Output

Print the minimum unfairness.

Example

Input:

5 2
8 15 10 20 8

Output:

31
solution:
n, k = map(int, input().split())
a = sorted(map(int, input().split()), reverse=True)
best = sum(a)
load = [0] * k
def go(i):
    global best
    if i == n:
        best = min(best, max(load))
        return
    seen = set()
    for j in range(k):
        if load[j] in seen or load[j] + a[i] >= best:
            continue
        seen.add(load[j])
        load[j] += a[i]
        go(i + 1)
        load[j] -= a[i]
go(0)
print(best)
